chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Faddal, from Tha'laba, from Sabbah al-Azraq, from Hakam al-Hannat, from Abu Basir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and Hakam from Ibn Abi Ya'fur from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) — they both said:

'Whoever judges regarding two dirhams by other than what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has revealed, from among those who have a whip or a staff (i.e., hold ruling authority), then he is a disbeliever in what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has revealed upon Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family).'

key_terms.دِرْهَمَيْنِ: Two dirhams — a minimal sum emphasizing that no case is too small to require divine law
key_terms.سَوْطٌ أَوْ عَصًا: A whip or a staff — metonymy for judicial or ruling authority
key_terms.كَافِرٌ: Disbeliever — used technically to denote one who acts in rejection of divine law
key_terms.مَنْ حَكَمَ بِغَيْرِ مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّه: Whoever judges by other than what Allah revealed — an explicit echo of Quran 5:44, 5:45, 5:47

ai.seo_question: What does Islam say about judging by other than what Allah revealed?
ai.summary: This hadith, reported through two parallel chains converging at both Imam al-Baqir and Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon them), delivers an extremely grave ruling: any judge or authority figure who renders a verdict — even in a trivial matter involving as little as two dirhams — by other than divine law is declared a disbeliever (kafir). The mention of 'whip or staff' signifies those holding coercive authority (i.e., judges, rulers, and enforcers). This teaching reinforced the Shia understanding that legitimate governance and adjudication must be grounded exclusively in the divine revelation as transmitted through the Imams.
